question.text: Mr. Rohan Desai, a top-slab resident LP (income > INR 5 crore), receives pass-through LTCG of INR 4 crore on unlisted equity shares from Bharat Private Equity Fund (Cat II, post-23-07-2024 exit). Compute his total tax (base + surcharge + cess), assuming the 15% surcharge cap on LTCG applies.

answer.text: INR 50,00,000 base + INR 7,50,000 surcharge + INR 2,30,000 cess = INR 59,80,000.
INR 80,00,000 base + INR 29,60,000 surcharge + INR 4,38,400 cess = INR 1,13,98,400.
INR 50,00,000 flat, no surcharge or cess.

explanation.text: The Logic: Base tax on unlisted-share LTCG (Section 112) = 4,00,00,000 x 12.5% = INR 50,00,000. Surcharge is CAPPED at 15% on LTCG (post-FA 2022) = 50,00,000 x 15% = INR 7,50,000. Health and Education Cess at 4% on (50,00,000 + 7,50,000) = 4% x 57,50,000 = INR 2,30,000. Total = 50,00,000 + 7,50,000 + 2,30,000 = INR 59,80,000. The Trap: Option B wrongly applies the 20% STCG rate to an LTCG, inflating everything. Option C applies the peak 37% surcharge, ignoring the 15% cap. Option D omits surcharge and cess entirely. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C tests this same computation. XXI-B tests it for PMS clients. X-B (IA L2) uses it for after-tax planning of HNI portfolios. The 15% cap is a major post-FA 2022 efficiency — do not miss it in fund IRR modelling. Manager's Pro-Tip: When modelling a 10-year PE fund IRR for anchor LPs, always split the exit-proceeds NPV into (a) LTCG on unlisted equity (12.5% + 15% capped surcharge = ~14.95% effective pre-cess) and (b) ordinary income on interest/coupons (up to 39% for top bracket). The character-mix can change after-tax IRR by 300+ bps.
